newsitem.title: USA: Mexico defends action on drug czar corruption case.
newsitem.headline: Mexico defends action on drug czar corruption case.

text.p: Mexico's foreign minister on Friday defended his country's response to corruption charges against its top drug enforcement official, and criticised the U.S. policy of certifying his country's anti-narcotics effort.

"The reason why we fight against drugs is not because we want to get a grade or a certification from anybody," Mexican Foreign Minister Jose Angel Gurria said at a news conference. "We think it in fact inhibits cooperation."

Mexico is among 32 countries facing U.S. certification at the end of this month in Washington's annual evaluation of other governments' actions against drug traffickings. Those that fail the test may face U.S. economic and trade sanctions.

Gurria was in Washington for meetings at the White House, the State Department and the Justice Department that coincided with international fallout over Tuesday's announcement that Mexican anti-drug chief Gen. Jesus Gutierrez Rebollo had been discharged from his post and charged with drug corruption.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Gurria got "several pieces of our mind" over the Gutierrez matter when Gurria met with presidential adviser Thomas "Mack" McLarty on Thursday.
And on Friday, a spokesman for the Senate Foreign Relations Committee said bluntly that Mexico should not get certification.
"We should decertify Mexico. Nothing short of decertifications show these countries that we are serious," spokesman Mark Thiessen said in a telephone interview.

President Bill Clinton said on Wednesday the Gutierrez case was "deeply troubling" for the United States but nevertheless praised Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo for acting swiftly to remove the tainted general.

Gutierrez, who had been head of Mexico's National Institute for Combating Drugs for 10 weeks, was ousted after government officials alleged that he had accepted bribes from Mexico's biggest drug mafia, the Juarez cartel.
"It's a very big blow to the process, we don't want to deny it, we don't want to minimise it," Gurria said, referring to the Gutierrez case. But he said there was no foot-dragging on Mexico's part.
"The moment we had all the elements (of the case) in our hands, we went public," Gurria said.

He said high-level U.S.-Mexican cooperation aimed at preventing drug trafficking was continuing, and in fact was a success, with numerous arrests of drug kingpins and large quantities of narcotics seized.
However, he acknowledged the temptation of easy money from drug lords was a problem for drug-interdiction officials.

"What we do is try to identify them all that we can and put them in jail," Gurria said. "But human nature, unfortunately, we cannot predict. There are very dedicated, very committed people who are faced every day with the temptation of getting a handful of dollars which represent a year or two of their salaries or more, and don't take it."
"And there are people who use the office to enrich themselves," he said. "We should salute the ones and put the others in jail. That's the only solution. We just have to keep on at it."
